title: The 'Pink Flags' of Postpartum Psychosis Every Family Should Know
excerpt: As the Lindsay Clancy trial grips the nation, psychiatrists urge families to recognize subtle warning signs before a mental health crisis escalates.
body:
• Postpartum psychosis is a rare psychiatric emergency affecting 1 to 2 in every 1,000 births, but experts say cases may be rising and the condition is widely underrecognized.
  • Psychiatrists now emphasize "pink flags" — subtle warning signs like severe insomnia, confusion, and irritability — that can precede full psychotic episodes and should trigger immediate medical evaluation.
  • The ongoing Lindsay Clancy murder trial in Massachusetts has thrust maternal mental health into the national conversation, with experts warning that the U.S. healthcare system routinely fails new mothers.
  • The condition is highly treatable with medication and hospitalization, and nearly all patients recover with proper care — but delayed diagnosis remains the biggest threat.

The murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, the 35-year-old former Massachusetts nurse accused of killing her three children in January 2023, has become the most closely watched criminal case in America this summer. But beyond the courtroom drama, mental health experts say the case is exposing a dangerous gap in how the U.S. healthcare system handles one of the most severe — and most treatable — psychiatric emergencies a new mother can face.

Clancy does not deny killing her children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan — in the family's Duxbury home before jumping from a second-story window, leaving her paralyzed from the waist down. Her defense argues she was suffering from undiagnosed postpartum psychosis, a condition that caused her to lose touch with reality. Prosecutors maintain the killings were deliberate and premeditated.

What Are the 'Pink Flags'?

Perinatal psychiatrist Dr. Uruj Kamal Haider, medical director of MCPAP for Moms in Massachusetts, is urging families to look beyond the dramatic symptoms most people associate with psychosis. In a recent episode of CBS's "Healthful" podcast with Norah O'Donnell, Dr. Haider introduced the concept of "pink flags" — the subtle, early warning signs that can precede a full psychotic break.

"There is a spectrum of psychotic symptoms, and the signs and symptoms can be very subtle, so I refer to these as pink flags," Dr. Haider told the New York Post. "Examples of pink flag signs may be irritability, disorganization, disorientation or confusion and rapid speech."

"These symptoms need to be taken seriously and treated immediately so they don't escalate into active psychosis."

— Dr. Uruj Kamal Haider, perinatal psychiatrist

Unlike the hallucinations and delusions that define full-blown psychosis, these early indicators — severe insomnia despite exhaustion, increased agitation, mood swings, and worsening confusion — can easily be dismissed as normal new-parent fatigue. Dr. Haider stresses that family members, spouses, and even neighbors need to learn these signs. "We need to learn how to support the village of the mother," she says.

A Condition That Waxes and Wanes

Part of what makes postpartum psychosis so dangerous is its unpredictable nature. Dr. Eboni January, a Nevada-based OB-GYN, says a mother can appear completely normal at a doctor's appointment and be in the grip of delusions hours later.

"Postpartum psychosis waxes and wanes, meaning a mom could be fine at 2 p.m. and then at 2 a.m. she's a completely different person, and that's why many times families miss it," Dr. January explains.

Compounding the problem: there is no standardized screening tool for postpartum psychosis, unlike the surveys routinely used for postpartum depression and anxiety. Most hospitals discharge new mothers within 48 hours of birth and schedule their next visit six weeks later. "The peak risk window for psychosis falls entirely inside that gap," says Claire Walker, a certified nurse-midwife in Indiana.

The Numbers Behind the Crisis

Postpartum psychosis is rare, affecting roughly 1 to 2 women per 1,000 births — about 0.1 to 0.2% of deliveries, compared with postpartum depression's rate of roughly 1 in 7 to 1 in 8 new mothers. But experts say recent data suggests the condition may be more common than previously believed, with a study tracking a small increase in cases between 2016 and 2019.

The stakes are enormous. According to Dr. Haider, 23% of maternal deaths in the United States are secondary to maternal mental health conditions, and research has shown nearly 100% of those deaths were preventable. Mental health conditions are now the leading cause of maternal mortality in the country.

Risk factors include a personal or family history of bipolar disorder, a prior episode of postpartum psychosis, discontinuation of mood-stabilizing medications during pregnancy, and severe sleep deprivation around childbirth. Genetics play a significant role: research shows that if a woman's sister had both postpartum psychosis and bipolar disorder, her risk multiplies 14 times. But roughly half of all cases occur in women with no prior psychiatric history.

A South Asian Survivor Speaks Out

Joining Dr. Haider on CBS's "Healthful" was Kriti Lodha, a South Asian-American marketing executive and postpartum psychosis survivor who has become one of the condition's most visible advocates. Lodha, who was diagnosed during the pandemic after a traumatic birth experience, now serves as Executive Advisor at the Center for Women's Mental Health at Massachusetts General Hospital and sits on the board of Postpartum Support International.

"It was a perfect storm of sleep deprivation, being a new mom, a traumatic birth experience, and it was really the postpartum period where the journey turned really dark for me," Lodha said on the podcast. "I was not of sound mind. I lost my mind. I was unfit to parent. I didn't know, frankly, if I'd ever come out of it."

"I was not of sound mind. I lost my mind. I was unfit to parent. I didn't know, frankly, if I'd ever come out of it."

— Kriti Lodha, postpartum psychosis survivor

Lodha's advocacy has focused on combating the stigma around postpartum psychosis, particularly within South Asian communities where mental health discussions remain taboo for many families. She has spoken publicly about the dichotomy of feeling isolated during the pandemic while also being supported by her South Asian community, and advocates for treating the diagnosis as a treatable medical condition rather than a sensationalized character flaw.

Similarly, postpartum psychosis advocate Aaisha Alvi, author of the memoir "A Mom Like That," has shared her own experience of being dismissed by multiple healthcare providers before finally receiving a correct diagnosis. "The difference between her outcome and Clancy's came down to being properly listened to," according to a Psychology Today analysis of both cases.

What to Do If You Suspect Postpartum Psychosis

Experts are unequivocal: postpartum psychosis is a medical emergency. Dr. January advises calling 911 immediately if you suspect a new mother is experiencing symptoms. "Don't wait. This is not an 'I'm going to call the office on Monday' situation," she says.

Dr. Jana Rundle, a perinatal psychologist, offers specific guidance for families: "If a mother is at home, will not willingly consent to treatment, and someone suspects postpartum psychosis, the safest next step is to call 911. When calling, be very specific: 'She recently gave birth, has barely slept, is confused or expressing beliefs that are not based in reality, and we are concerned about postpartum psychosis.'"

Critically, experts advise never leaving a mother alone with or without her baby during a suspected episode, keeping the environment calm, removing anything that could be used impulsively, and avoiding arguments about her delusions.

Treatment typically includes antipsychotic medications, mood stabilizers like lithium, and in some cases electroconvulsive therapy. With proper care, nearly all patients make a full recovery. "It is a very, very treatable condition," says Dr. Veerle Bergink, director of the Women's Mental Health Center at Mount Sinai. "There are women who have this as a single episode in their lives. They get severely ill — and never again."

What Comes Next

The Clancy trial, which began on July 27 and is expected to last several weeks, will likely hinge on whether the jury accepts the defense's argument that she was not criminally responsible due to postpartum psychosis. If found not guilty by reason of insanity under Massachusetts law, Clancy would face an indefinite stay in a secure state mental health facility, not release.

Regardless of the verdict, experts hope the case catalyzes real change. The U.S. currently offers most new mothers just one postpartum check-up at six weeks — a timeline that misses the highest-risk window for psychosis entirely. Postpartum psychosis is not recognized as a standalone diagnosis in the DSM, the standard manual for mental health diagnoses, making it harder for providers to identify and treat.

"Postpartum psychosis is a medical illness with a biological basis, not a character flaw and not a failure of love," says Walker. For families, recognizing the pink flags may be the difference between a crisis and a recovery.

If you or someone you know is experiencing a mental health crisis, call the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by dialing 988, or contact the Postpartum Support International helpline at 1-800-944-4773.
